outcome: No accepted resolution exists as of 11 Oct 2026. The record holds a 2019 unrefereed claim of convergence (Carella) that no later paper I found engages with, a 2025 claim of convergence withdrawn by a co-author in Sept 2026, 2025-2026 preprints that still call the classical series open or conditional, and a 6 Oct 2026 OpenAI release (repository openai/math, family 017, manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026) whose manuscript proves that the irrationality exponent of pi is 2 and states convergence of the classical Flint Hills series as a corollary. The Lean-checked statement covers the exponent only; the repository itself says the convergence consequence is outside it. I found no public check of the corollary by a named mathematician.
problem_asks: The statement asks one question: whether the Flint Hills series converges. The frozen bullet gives no formula, so the series is taken as the one the literature calls the Flint Hills series: the sum over n = 1, 2, 3, ... of 1/(n^3 sin^2 n), with sin in radians (Pickover 2002, as cited by Alekseyev 2011 and MathWorld). Parts: (a) decide whether the partial sums of this series have a finite limit. The terms are positive, so the only alternative is divergence (partial sums tend to infinity). The bullet asks convergence: it does not ask for the value of the sum, the rate of divergence, or the behaviour of the individual terms.

events.what_happened: N. A. Carella, 'Irrationality Measure of Pi', arXiv:1902.08817 (math.GM). First posted 23 Feb 2019; latest version v10 posted 12 May 2022. Claims (Theorem 1.1) that the irrationality measure mu(pi) = 2. Claims (Theorem 10.1, restated as Theorem 12.1; Example 10.1) that for u, v > 0 with u - v > 0 the series sum 1/(n^u |sin n|^v) is absolutely convergent, and applies this with u = 3, v = 2 (u - v = 1) to conclude that sum 1/(n^3 sin^2 n) converges. The paper's keywords include 'Flint Hills series'. Read via the ar5iv HTML of the latest version; I did not check whether v1 already contained the Flint Hills section.
events.revisions: v1 23 Feb 2019; latest v10 12 May 2022 (version list read from the arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Claims that the classical series converges, by the general absolute-convergence theorem for u - v > 0 (Theorem 10.1 as stated in the paper), and claims mu(pi) = 2. Both claims are the paper's own; the Flint Hills convergence rests on a step the paper asserts ('|1/sin(p_n)| <= c_1 p_n') without a derivation in the text I read.
events.remains: Nothing, if the claims held. The paper does not reconcile its claim mu(pi) = 2 with the bounds it cites itself (Salikhov's 7.6063 and Zeilberger-Zudilin's 7.103205...), as read in the ar5iv text.
events.doubts: (1) Unrefereed; no journal publication found. (2) The Flint Hills convergence step is asserted without derivation in the text read (Theorem 10.1: '|1/sin(p_n)| <= c_1 p_n'). (3) The claimed mu(pi) = 2 would be a major result; the paper's own cited bounds (7.6063, 7.103205) do not match it, and the paper does not address this (ar5iv text). (4) A search excerpt (not opened) reports that Chen and Pearse proved mu(pi) = 2 only under an extra limsup condition and that the full statement is open. (5) Every 2011-2026 paper I read that addresses the classical series (Alekseyev, Meiburg, Agama, Garab, Lopez Zapata, Dan) calls it open, and none of them engages with Carella's argument (Lopez Zapata's v5 reference list does not include it).
events.direction: Claims convergence of the classical series (answer 'yes' to the bullet) and claims mu(pi) = 2.

events.what_happened: Doron Zeilberger and Wadim Zudilin, 'The Irrationality Measure of Pi is at most 7.103205334137...', arXiv:1912.06345, first submitted 13 Dec 2019. Proves mu(pi) <= 7.103205334137..., a variant of Salikhov's method. The abstract does not mention the Flint Hills series. A search excerpt (msp.org; not opened) gives publication in Moscow Journal of Combinatorics and Number Theory 9 (2020), 407-419.
events.delivers: An upper bound mu(pi) <= 7.103205334137.... It bears on the Flint Hills problem only through the threshold 5/2 (Alekseyev, Meiburg): 7.10 is far above 5/2, so this bound does not move the convergence question.
events.remains: The whole question: mu(pi) is not known to be below 5/2, and the series is not decided by this bound.

checked_by.who: Moscow Journal of Combinatorics and Number Theory (journal of record)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, per a search excerpt (msp.org). I did not open the journal page.

events.direction: Upper bound on mu(pi); no direction on convergence.

events.what_happened: Max A. Alekseyev, 'On convergence of the Flint Hills series', arXiv:1104.5100 (math.CA, cross-listed math.NT). Submitted 27 Apr 2011. States that it is not known whether the series converges (abstract); proves (Corollary 4) that if the series converges then mu(pi) <= 5/2; treats the family sum 1/(n^u |sin n|^v) and gives conditions on u, v in terms of the then-known bound on mu(pi). Attributes the Flint Hills series to Pickover. No journal publication found in searches.
events.revisions: v1 27 Apr 2011 (only version listed on the abstract page read).
events.delivers: A necessary condition, not a resolution: convergence of the classical series implies mu(pi) <= 5/2, equivalently mu(pi) > 5/2 implies divergence. The paper's series-convergence theorem for sum 1/(n^u |sin n|^v) (Theorem 5, as read in the ar5iv text) needs mu(pi) < 1 + (u - 1)/v, which for u = 3, v = 2 is mu(pi) < 2; every irrational has mu >= 2, so that theorem gives nothing for pi. Its Theorem 2 concerns the terms tending to zero under mu < 1 + u/v, not the convergence of the series.
events.remains: Whether the series converges; in particular the range 2 <= mu(pi) < 5/2 is not settled by this paper.
events.doubts: Later papers credit Alekseyev with more than the text I read supports: Lopez Zapata (v5, Section 1) says 'Alekseyev proved that the series converges if mu(pi) < 5/2', and DeepMind formal-conjectures issue 6909 says 'Alekseyev showed that mu(pi) < 5/2 implies convergence'. The 5/2 sufficiency appears in Meiburg (2022) and in Lopez Zapata's Corollary 5, not in the 2011 text as read.
events.direction: Necessary condition only: convergence would force mu(pi) <= 5/2. Leaves the question open.

events.what_happened: Theophilus Agama, 'On the flint hills series', arXiv:2109.00295 (math.GM). v1 submitted 1 Sep 2021; v2 revised 13 Apr 2026 ('the paper has been reformatted and introduction expanded; a mind picture of the iteration method supplied'). Uses an iteration method that places pillars near the terms and relates the series to modified series. Theorem 3.1: if for some s in N and every small epsilon > 0 the 2s-th power of a double binomial sum G(n) is at most |sin^2 n| times n^(2s+2-epsilon), then the series converges. The abstract says the convergence 'relies very heavily on the condition', and the paper does not claim to resolve the problem.
events.revisions: v1 1 Sep 2021; v2 13 Apr 2026 (reformatted, introduction expanded; abstract and theorem statement otherwise as read).
events.delivers: A conditional sufficient condition for convergence: convergence follows if the stated binomial-sum inequality holds. The paper does not show that the inequality holds for the series, so it does not settle the problem.
events.remains: Whether the binomial-sum inequality holds, and hence convergence.
events.doubts: The key inequality is not verified in the text read; the paper describes its criterion as a 'test tool'. No public engagement found.
events.direction: Conditional sufficient condition for convergence; no answer.

events.what_happened: Alex Meiburg, 'Bounds on Irrationality Measures and the Flint-Hills Series', arXiv:2208.13356 (math.NT, 12 pages). Submitted 29 Aug 2022; no later versions listed. Introduction: 'Our main result is a near-complete converse, that if mu(pi) < 5/2, then the Flint-Hills series converges.' Theorem 2.5: for a sine-like function P with irrational period alpha, constant v >= 1, and mu(alpha) < 1 + u/v, the series S_{u,v}(n) converges. The Flint Hills series is the instance alpha = pi, P = |sin|, u = 3, v = 2, giving mu(pi) < 5/2. Section 3: at mu(alpha) = 1 + u/v there is a divergence example for some irrational alpha, and the case mu(pi) = 5/2 'will leave unanswered whether or not the Flint Hill series converges'. Conjecture 3.1 (convergence at equality) is stated as unproven. The abstract says the boundary case is 'briefly addressed, with evidence that it would be hard to resolve'.
events.revisions: v1 29 Aug 2022; no later versions listed on the abstract page read.
events.delivers: Convergence of the classical series for every irrationality measure of pi below 5/2, provided mu(pi) < 5/2 holds; in particular it covers 2 <= mu(pi) < 5/2. Restrictions: conditional on an upper bound mu(pi) < 5/2, which is not known (best known upper bound about 7.10); the equality case mu(pi) = 5/2 is left open; the paper's own text marks Theorems 2.1 and 3.1 as proved in full and Theorems 2.2-2.4 as cited from Alekseyev.
events.remains: The bullet's question for the actual value of mu(pi): this result converts the question into whether mu(pi) < 5/2, which is open; also the case mu(pi) = 5/2, and Meiburg's Conjecture 3.1.
events.doubts: (1) Unrefereed preprint; no journal publication found. (2) Garab (arXiv 2510.27041, Oct 2025) cites Meiburg, and its Section 6 says that if mu(pi) < 2.5 the series converges, yet its Section 3.1 says 'The intermediate range 2.37 <= mu(pi) <= 2.5 remains undecided'. Those two statements cannot both be read as Garab's settled view, and I did not find a published gap in Meiburg's argument that explains the Section 3.1 statement. (3) Lopez Zapata (v5, Sept 2026) does not cite Meiburg and attributes the 5/2 sufficiency to Alekseyev, so the sufficiency is asserted by two unrefereed papers (Meiburg; Lopez Zapata via Corollary 5) and questioned in one (Garab Section 3.1).
events.direction: Convergence for mu(pi) < 5/2 (cuts toward 'converges'), conditional on that inequality, which is not established. Divergence for mu > 5/2 is credited to Alekseyev. Silent at mu(pi) = 5/2.
events.object: Theorem 3.1 gives, at the critical exponent mu = 1 + u/v, the existence (not an explicit construction, per the paper's wording 'at least alpha_2 exists') of an irrational alpha for which the series can diverge. This concerns alpha generally, not alpha = pi.

events.what_happened: Cahlen Humphreys, 'Flint Hills Series: Partial Sums to 10^10 with Spike Decomposition', bigcompute.science web page dated 29 Mar 2026. Computes the partial sum to N = 10^10 (value 30.31454612, one GPU, 1.9 s), decomposes it into 19 spike terms in quad-double precision and a smooth bulk, and states that the data 'provides empirical evidence for the hypothesis that spikes decay'. The page says 'Convergence is not proved' and that the convergence direction is 'conditional on Open Problem 5.6' (a numbering from Lopez Zapata's papers; the version I read of that paper does not contain it). Lopez Zapata's v5 cites this page as reference [2].
events.delivers: Numerical partial sums to N = 10^10 and a spike decomposition of the sum. It establishes no convergence result: finitely many partial sums do not decide convergence of a series, and the page says so.

checked_by.who: Page header: 'AI-audited, not peer-reviewed' (the auditing system is not named on the page)
checked_by.what_they_did: Audit of the page, per its header; not a mathematical referee report

events.directly_checkable: The partial sums to 10^10 can be recomputed; the page gives the stated value 30.31454612. The page reports GPU and precision details.
events.doubts: Numerical evidence only; the page itself says convergence is not proved.
events.direction: Numerical evidence for convergence; no proof.

I did not read the v1 body text; the v2 HTML URL returned 404.

events.remains: All of the question, as withdrawn.

The withdrawal note says: 'the partial-sum argument does not prove Flint--Hills convergence'; 'Hölder continuity alone does not establish the proof' (quoted in an earlier fetch of the same note); 'Eq. (1.1) has a numerical error'.

events.what_happened: Mohammed-Adnane Garab, 'A Geometric-Arithmetic Framework for the Flint Hills Series', arXiv:2510.27041 (single author). One version, submitted 30 Oct 2025. Defines d(n) = dist(n, pi Z) and a two-sided bound L(N) <= S_N <= G(N) on partial sums (Theorem 2.1; the paper states that S converges iff L(N) converges). Theorem 6.1: there is a constant mu_0 with 2.37 <= mu_0 <= 2.5 such that mu(pi) < mu_0 is equivalent to convergence of the auxiliary series sum 1/(n^3 d(n)^2); the paper says 'if mu(pi) < 2.37 then the Flint Hills series converges, while if mu(pi) > 2.5 then it diverges', supported only by an 'Idea of the proof' ('Details and refinements will appear elsewhere'). Corollary 2.2: for every eta > 0 the weighted series sum 1/(n^(3+eta) sin^2 n) converges (a different series). Proposition 3.1 is labelled heuristic.
events.delivers: (a) For the weighted series with exponent 3 + eta, eta > 0: convergence (Corollary 2.2). That is an analogue and settles nothing about the bullet's series. (b) A reduction of the classical series to an auxiliary series (Theorem 2.1), and a conditional threshold statement (Theorem 6.1, with an idea-only proof). Restriction: the classical case is left open; the paper says 'Despite many attempts, it is still unknown whether S converges.'
events.remains: Convergence of the classical series; and mu(pi) in the range [2.37, 2.5] per the paper's own Section 3.1.
events.doubts: (1) Internal inconsistency, quoted from the HTML: Section 3.1 'The intermediate range 2.37 <= mu(pi) <= 2.5 remains undecided'; Section 6 'We recall that if mu(pi) < 2.5 then, as noted above, the Flint Hills series converges.' (2) Theorem 6.1 is supported only by an 'Idea of the proof'. (3) Corollary 2.2's proof relies on 'a standard equidistribution argument' for the second set of indices. (4) Proposition 3.1 is heuristic ('Although the above argument is heuristic...').
events.direction: Conditional and partial: the analogue converges; the classical question is left open by the paper.

events.what_happened: Carlos H. Lopez Zapata, 'A Continued-Fraction Criterion for the Flint Hills Series, and the Integer Sequences It Generates', arXiv:2603.09719 (math.GM). Five versions. The version read (v5, 13 Sep 2026, 'Expanded 9 page version with 2 tables') states: the series converges if and only if a sum of squared consecutive partial quotients, each divided by the corresponding convergent denominator, is finite (criterion for the continued fraction of 1/pi). Corollary 5: Theta(alpha) = mu(alpha) - 2; if Theta(alpha) < 1/2 then the series D(alpha) converges (the paper's notation), so mu(pi) < 5/2 would give convergence. The v5 text says 'whether it converges is a well-known open problem' (abstract) and 'The convergence therefore remains undecided' (Section 1), and 'A proof that mu(pi) < 5/2 would establish convergence, but the available bounds on mu(pi) are far from this value' (Section 3).
events.revisions: v1 10 Mar 2026; v2 11 Mar 2026 (10 KB); v3 15 Mar 2026 (15 KB); v4 20 Apr 2026 (48 KB); v5 13 Sep 2026 (9 KB, 'Expanded 9 page version with 2 tables'). I read only v5's HTML and abstract listing. Search excerpts describe earlier versions with an unconditional identity S = (4/3) zeta(3) + (1/3) R_1* and an 'Open Problem 5.6' with a case split at 2 <= mu < 5/2; v5 does not contain Theorem 5.5 or Open Problem 5.6 as far as my fetch shows, so those earlier claims are unverified here.
events.delivers: A criterion (equivalence) for convergence in terms of the partial quotients of 1/pi, and a sufficient condition for convergence (Corollary 5) when mu(pi) < 5/2. Restriction: the criterion is stated as an equivalence by the author, but the author itself says the convergence question remains undecided because the condition on mu(pi) is not known.
events.remains: Whether the continued-fraction sum is finite for 1/pi, equivalently whether mu(pi) < 5/2 (not known). The problem's question is not settled by the paper.
events.doubts: (1) The criterion and Corollary 5 are the author's; no referee or public check found. (2) Versions differ materially: earlier-version excerpts (search only) claim more (an unconditional identity; an Open Problem 5.6 that a March 2026 page cites as the remaining step), and v5 does not contain those items as far as I read. The record should be checked against the version the later pass is using. (3) Corollary 5 is the same threshold sufficiency as Meiburg's, cited by Lopez Zapata only through Alekseyev.
events.direction: Criterion and a sufficient condition (mu(pi) < 5/2) for convergence; the author states the question remains undecided.

events.what_happened: Yuya Dan, 'Critical convergence and Hausdorff measures for generalized Flint Hills series', arXiv:2609.12338 (math.NT, 18 pages, MSC 11J82, 11J70, 11J83, 11K50, 28A78). Single version submitted 11 Sep 2026. Studies F_{s,t}(x) = sum n^(-s) |sin(pi n x)|^(-t) for s > 0, t > 1: Hausdorff dimension of the divergence set min{1, 2t/(s+t)}; numbers of irrationality exponent tau = 1 + s/t that realise both convergence and divergence; claims the convergent examples establish Meiburg's conjecture for t > 1. The abstract says that the convergence of the classical Flint Hills series 'remains undecided'.
events.delivers: Results on a generalised family F_{s,t} (critical exponents, divergence dimension, Hausdorff measures). This is an analogue, not the classical series, so under the scope test it settles nothing for the bullet. The classical case is described by the author as undecided.
events.remains: The classical series (the paper's own abstract says undecided).

events.what_happened: OpenAI release, public repository openai/math (Apache-2.0), published 6 Oct 2026 per press reports and an embedded OpenAI post. Family 017, 'The irrationality exponent of pi is 2', with a manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026 (repository path preprints/The-irrationality-exponent-of-pi-is-2-September-24-2026/paper.pdf). The manuscript abstract, as quoted in the repository's CONTENTS.md, says: 'We prove the conjecture that the irrationality exponent of pi is 2' and 'As a consequence, the classical Flint-Hills series sum_{n>=1} 1/(n^3 sin^2 n) converges, with angles in radians.' The repository's family-017 Lean page (pinned commit adc7f12) says the formalization 'proves that the irrationality exponent of pi is exactly two', comparator statement 'The irrationality exponent of pi equals two', and that 'The paper's convergence consequence for the Flint-Hills series is outside this selected statement.' I could not read the manuscript PDF (binary; the fetch tool returned no text), so I have not seen its proof of the corollary or its route from mu(pi) = 2 to convergence.
events.revisions: Repository pinned at commit adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a (the family-017 Lean page is at that commit). Manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026 by its repository path. I did not open the repository's history.md. I chose 6 Oct 2026 as the first public date because it is the earliest public appearance I found; the manuscript's own date is 24 Sep 2026.
events.delivers: Claims that mu(pi) = 2 (the exact irrationality exponent of pi), and that the classical series converges as a corollary. The Lean-checked statement covers only the exponent claim. The convergence step therefore rests on the manuscript's informal argument and on a threshold theorem for mu(pi) < 5/2 that is itself unrefereed (Meiburg 2022, Theorem 2.5; or Lopez Zapata 2026, Corollary 5). Which of these the manuscript uses I could not confirm.
events.remains: Nothing, if the corollary holds. The corollary is not covered by the Lean check, and its dependence on the 5/2 threshold theorem has no public check I could find.

events.directly_checkable: The corollary is a claim about the series 1/(n^3 sin^2 n). The exponent claim is that |pi - p/q| >= q^(-nu) for every nu > 2 and all sufficiently large q, for every integer p. Neither was checked by me by hand. The Lean file covers the exponent claim only; I did not open PiExponent.lean. A secondary source says the challenge file 'deliberately contains the target theorem with a placeholder proof', so a sorry in that challenge file is expected and does not itself show a gap.
events.doubts: (1) The convergence corollary is outside the Lean-checked statement (repository scope note, quoted above). (2) The corollary needs the threshold theorem mu(pi) < 5/2 => convergence. The sources for it are unrefereed (Meiburg 2022; Lopez Zapata 2026 Corollary 5). Garab (Oct 2025) says the range 2.37 <= mu(pi) <= 2.5 is undecided, while the same paper's Section 6 says mu(pi) < 2.5 gives convergence; I did not resolve that conflict. (3) mu(pi) = 2 would be a jump from the best known bound of about 7.10 to the exact value. A Universitas Scholarium essay (Oct 2026) calls this 'either a new idea or a mistake' and names no specific error. (4) The repository README warns that unformalised results 'could have issues'. (5) DeepMind formal-conjectures issue 6909 (opened 7 Oct 2026; the issue says 'The comparison was prepared with AI assistance and may contain mistakes') proposes marking the Flint Hills entry as solved and attributes 'mu(pi) < 5/2 implies convergence' to Alekseyev; the 2011 text I read does not support that attribution as stated (see the alekseyev-2011-04 doubts). (6) Secondary catalogues disagree on whether the family-017 main result is Lean-formalized ('Yes' on Emergent Mind; 'Not yet' in one catalogue quoted in a search excerpt).
events.direction: Yes: the classical series converges (claimed as a corollary). The claim also asserts mu(pi) = 2, which is the threshold condition that the 2022 and 2026 papers use.

events.what_happened: The single manuscript, 'The irrationality exponent of pi is 2' (build/main.tex), claims two results. (1) Theorem 1.1 (thm:main): for every real ν>2 there is an integer Q(ν) such that |π − p/q| ≥ q^(−ν) for all integers p and all integers q ≥ Q(ν); fractions need not be reduced. With the pigeonhole bound μ(π) ≥ 2 this gives μ(π) = 2. (2) Corollary 1.2 (thm:flinthills): the classical Flint–Hills series Σ_{n≥1} 1/(n³ sin²n), angles in radians, converges. The corollary is proved in sections/series.tex. Fix ν in (2, 5/2); Theorem 1.1 gives ‖qπ‖ ≥ c·q^(1−ν) for all q ≥ 1, with c > 0 absorbing the finitely many q below Q. A dyadic spacing lemma (series:dyadic) turns this into Σ 1/(q³‖qπ‖²) < ∞. Each n is grouped by its nearest multiple q of π, and each group's contribution is bounded by (8/π)/(q³‖qπ‖²). The proof does not use the cited Alekseyev (μ ≤ 5/2 is necessary) or Meiburg (μ < 5/2 is sufficient) results. The same manuscript also states Corollary (series:generalized): for fixed a, b > 0, Σ 1/(n^a |sin n|^b) with angles in radians converges if and only if a > max{1, b}. The abstract and introduction present both results as proved.
events.delivers: Convergence of the classical Flint–Hills series 1/(n³ sin²n), angles in radians: the manuscript claims the answer to the question is yes. Its framing matches the problem_asks reading. The introduction states the problem as whether Σ 1/(n³ sin²n) converges with angles in radians, and the claim answers that question affirmatively. The only hypothesis is the manuscript's own Theorem 1.1. That theorem's threshold Q(ν) is ineffective, but convergence needs only existence. The generalized criterion (a > max{1, b}) goes beyond the problem's single series.
events.remains: Nothing that problem_asks requires. The bullet asks only whether the series converges. The manuscript gives no value of the sum, no rate of the tail, and no explicit threshold Q(ν).

machine_checked.scope:
The formalization proves that the irrationality exponent of $\pi$ is exactly two. For every $\nu>2$, all sufficiently large positive denominators $q$ satisfy $|\pi-p/q|\ge q^{-\nu}$ for every integer numerator $p$. It also states the exact supremum characterization using infinitely many rational approximations.

The paper's convergence consequence for the Flint–Hills series is outside this selected statement.

events.doubts: No step is flagged as sketched, and the abstract, Corollary 1.2 and its proof contain no hedges. Points that bear on trust: (a) the manuscript states that the threshold Q(ν) in Theorem 1.1 is not given effectively (main.tex, lines 74–75); (b) the proof of Theorem 1.1 rests on a new separated-weight interpolation theorem (sections/interpolation.tex) that the paper proves itself rather than citing, and the outline says a dimension count alone does not establish the needed full-rank statement (main.tex, lines 183–185); the Flint–Hills claim inherits whatever holds for that argument; (c) the task's description of the repository's Lean formalisation (lean/docs/017.md) says it covers the exponent-two statement but not the Flint–Hills consequence, so by that description the convergence step is not formally covered. I did not open the Lean file.

disputes.summary: Carella (arXiv 1902.08817, first posted 2019) claims both mu(pi) = 2 and that the classical series converges (Theorem 10.1, Example 10.1). The OpenAI family-017 manuscript (dated 24 Sep 2026, released 6 Oct 2026) claims mu(pi) = 2 and convergence as a corollary. Neither is refereed; I found no source reconciling the two and I do not pick a winner.

Who established that mu(pi) < 5/2 implies convergence. Meiburg (2022, Theorem 2.5) states it. Lopez Zapata (v5, Sept 2026) credits Alekseyev and derives it via its Corollary 5. DeepMind formal-conjectures issue 6909 credits Alekseyev. Alekseyev's 2011 text, as I read it, gives series convergence only under mu < 2 (Theorem 5) and gives the 5/2 threshold only as a necessary condition (Corollary 4).

Garab (arXiv 2510.27041) says the range 2.37 <= mu(pi) <= 2.5 remains undecided (Section 3.1) and also that mu(pi) < 2.5 implies convergence (Section 6). Garab cites Meiburg (2022), whose Theorem 2.5 covers mu < 5/2. I did not find a published gap in Meiburg's argument that would explain Garab's Section 3.1.

Mantzakouras and Lopez Zapata (arXiv 2502.03474 v1, Jan 2025) claimed a proof of convergence; the note withdrawing v2 (Sept 2026) says the argument does not prove convergence. A Moonlight literature review (not opened; HTTP 429) reports the same claim with a value of about 30.31. The bigcompute numerics converge to about 30.3145 and the page says convergence is not proved. Apart from Carella (2019) and the OpenAI release, every source I read that addresses the classical series calls it open or conditional.

Secondary catalogues disagree on whether the Lean main result for family 017 is formalised: Emergent Mind marks the Lean formalization 'Yes'; a catalogue quoted in a search excerpt marks it 'Not yet'. The repository's family-017 page says the formalization proves the exponent statement and that the Flint Hills consequence is outside it.

summary: Status and what happened. As of 11 Oct 2026 no accepted resolution of the Flint Hills convergence question exists in the sources I could reach. Apart from the withdrawn 2025 claim (Mantzakouras and Lopez Zapata v1) and the 2019 claim by Carella, the human-authored 2025-2026 sources I read still describe the classical series as open or conditional (Garab 2025, Lopez Zapata v5 Sept 2026, Dan Sept 2026, the MathWorld text, which cites the 2025 preprint, and the DeepMind formal-conjectures entry as of March 2026). The events, in date order: Carella (2019) claimed convergence and mu(pi) = 2 without engagement from later papers; Alekseyev (2011) showed that convergence would force mu(pi) <= 5/2; Agama (2021, v2 2026) gave a conditional criterion; Meiburg (2022) proved convergence for mu(pi) < 5/2 (unrefereed; Theorem 2.5); Humphreys (Mar 2026) gave numerical partial sums to 10^10 and says convergence is not proved; Mantzakouras and Lopez Zapata (Jan 2025) claimed convergence and withdrew v2 in Sept 2026; Garab (Oct 2025) gave a conditional reduction and a weighted analogue; Lopez Zapata (Mar-Sept 2026) gave a continued-fraction criterion and a sufficient condition at mu < 5/2 and called the question undecided; Dan (Sept 2026) treated a generalised family and called the classical case undecided; Bai (Sept 2026) lowered the bound on mu(pi) to 7.101862832357, which does not reach 5/2; and OpenAI (manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026, released 6 Oct 2026) claims mu(pi) = 2 and, as a corollary, convergence of the classical series. The OpenAI claim is the one that would change the bullet's status if accepted. I could read its repository pages (the family-017 Lean scope note and the CONTENTS abstract line) but not the manuscript PDF, so I could not see its proof of the corollary or its route from mu(pi) = 2 to convergence. The repository's own Lean page says the convergence consequence is outside the Lean-checked statement. The convergence step, if it goes through Meiburg's Theorem 2.5 or Lopez Zapata's Corollary 5, rests on unrefereed preprints; Garab's own Section 3.1 calls the 2.37-2.5 range undecided. Alekseyev's 2011 text, as I read it, does not give the 5/2 sufficiency that several later sources credit to it; I record that conflict and do not resolve it in the events. Dates: the OpenAI event is dated 6 Oct 2026, the first public appearance I found, while the manuscript itself is dated 24 Sep 2026. The AI picture: the OpenAI release is produced by an 'unreleased internal OpenAI model' (repository README), which is the main AI involvement and is load-bearing for the claimed corollary; Bai (Sept 2026) credits 'GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra' with proof development and checking of the bound on mu(pi), a bound that does not bear on convergence; Dan (Sept 2026) credits Claude and ChatGPT with ideas in the generalised-series results; Humphreys (Mar 2026) credits Claude with 'human-AI collaboration' on numerical work without saying what Claude did. Other events name no AI system. Not included in ai.systems: the explanatory section that Emergent Mind attributes to 'GPT-6 Astra Medium' (secondhand, and explanatory rather than mathematics), which I could not check against the repository text. The problem's Wikipedia article: 'Flint Hills series' is a redirect to 'Series (mathematics)' (fetched Oct 2026), so the problem has no article of its own; the article I read in its first 100,000 characters does not mention the series. Pickover's 2002 book is the origin of the name and is not an event.
competing_reading: Reading the OpenAI release as settling the bullet: mu(pi) = 2 < 5/2 would give convergence through Meiburg's Theorem 2.5 (the fetched text gives it a complete proof in Section 3) or Lopez Zapata's Corollary 5 (his Theta = mu - 2 < 1/2 identity). On that reading the bullet's answer is 'converges', and the Lean gap is a formalization gap, not a mathematical one. The opposing reading: the corollary is not established. It rests on an unrefereed manuscript whose convergence step is outside the Lean check, on threshold theorems that have no referee report and that one of the 2025 papers calls undecided in part of the range, and on a claim (mu(pi) = 2) that would overturn the best known bound (about 7.10) with no public expert check. Under that reading the bullet remains open, with one claimed resolution in an unrefereed repository.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The manuscript family-017 PDF (preprints/The-irrationality-exponent-of-pi-is-2-September-24-2026/paper.pdf) read in full: which threshold theorem it uses for the corollary, and whether it proves the step from mu(pi) = 2 to convergence of sum 1/(n^3 sin^2 n). I could not read it with the tools available. (2) A named expert's check of the mu(pi) = 2 proof; the Lean file covers only the exponent. (3) A Lean formalization of the corollary itself, built from the repository, with its sorry status stated. (4) A referee assessment of Meiburg (2022) Theorem 2.5 in the range 2 <= mu(pi) < 5/2, which would settle whether Garab's Section 3.1 is a real gap or an error. (5) For the record: which version of Lopez Zapata's paper (arXiv 2603.09719) the 'Open Problem 5.6' citation refers to, since v5 does not contain it.

event.what_happened: OpenAI release, public repository openai/math (Apache-2.0), published 6 Oct 2026 per press reports and an embedded OpenAI post. Family 017, 'The irrationality exponent of pi is 2', with a manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026 (repository path preprints/The-irrationality-exponent-of-pi-is-2-September-24-2026/paper.pdf). The manuscript abstract, as quoted in the repository's CONTENTS.md, says: 'We prove the conjecture that the irrationality exponent of pi is 2' and 'As a consequence, the classical Flint-Hills series sum_{n>=1} 1/(n^3 sin^2 n) converges, with angles in radians.' The repository's family-017 Lean page (pinned commit adc7f12) says the formalization 'proves that the irrationality exponent of pi is exactly two', comparator statement 'The irrationality exponent of pi equals two', and that 'The paper's convergence consequence for the Flint-Hills series is outside this selected statement.' I could not read the manuscript PDF (binary; the fetch tool returned no text), so I have not seen its proof of the corollary or its route from mu(pi) = 2 to convergence.
event.revisions: Repository pinned at commit adc7f1241b42e322a6451854ab7e4b4c146bf78a (the family-017 Lean page is at that commit). Manuscript dated 24 Sep 2026 by its repository path. I did not open the repository's history.md. I chose 6 Oct 2026 as the first public date because it is the earliest public appearance I found; the manuscript's own date is 24 Sep 2026.
event.delivers: Claims that mu(pi) = 2 (the exact irrationality exponent of pi), and that the classical series converges as a corollary. The Lean-checked statement covers only the exponent claim. The convergence step therefore rests on the manuscript's informal argument and on a threshold theorem for mu(pi) < 5/2 that is itself unrefereed (Meiburg 2022, Theorem 2.5; or Lopez Zapata 2026, Corollary 5). Which of these the manuscript uses I could not confirm.
event.remains: Nothing, if the corollary holds. The corollary is not covered by the Lean check, and its dependence on the 5/2 threshold theorem has no public check I could find.

event.directly_checkable: The corollary is a claim about the series 1/(n^3 sin^2 n). The exponent claim is that |pi - p/q| >= q^(-nu) for every nu > 2 and all sufficiently large q, for every integer p. Neither was checked by me by hand. The Lean file covers the exponent claim only; I did not open PiExponent.lean. A secondary source says the challenge file 'deliberately contains the target theorem with a placeholder proof', so a sorry in that challenge file is expected and does not itself show a gap.
event.doubts: (1) The convergence corollary is outside the Lean-checked statement (repository scope note, quoted above). (2) The corollary needs the threshold theorem mu(pi) < 5/2 => convergence. The sources for it are unrefereed (Meiburg 2022; Lopez Zapata 2026 Corollary 5). Garab (Oct 2025) says the range 2.37 <= mu(pi) <= 2.5 is undecided, while the same paper's Section 6 says mu(pi) < 2.5 gives convergence; I did not resolve that conflict. (3) mu(pi) = 2 would be a jump from the best known bound of about 7.10 to the exact value. A Universitas Scholarium essay (Oct 2026) calls this 'either a new idea or a mistake' and names no specific error. (4) The repository README warns that unformalised results 'could have issues'. (5) DeepMind formal-conjectures issue 6909 (opened 7 Oct 2026; the issue says 'The comparison was prepared with AI assistance and may contain mistakes') proposes marking the Flint Hills entry as solved and attributes 'mu(pi) < 5/2 implies convergence' to Alekseyev; the 2011 text I read does not support that attribution as stated (see the alekseyev-2011-04 doubts). (6) Secondary catalogues disagree on whether the family-017 main result is Lean-formalized ('Yes' on Emergent Mind; 'Not yet' in one catalogue quoted in a search excerpt).
event.direction: Yes: the classical series converges (claimed as a corollary). The claim also asserts mu(pi) = 2, which is the threshold condition that the 2022 and 2026 papers use.

judgement.why: The statement asks only whether the series converges, so only a claim of unconditional convergence is 'whole'. Bounds on mu(pi) (Zeilberger-Zudilin, Bai) do not reach 5/2 and move no quantity the statement names, and threshold or criterion results (Alekseyev, Agama, Meiburg, Lopez Zapata) are reductions to unproven conditions, so all are 'none'. Garab's weighted series and Dan's generalised family are variants; Humphreys' partial sums are instances. Carella is set aside as not credible (several F10 signals together), and Mantzakouras-Lopez Zapata is knocked down by the co-author's withdrawal. The OpenAI claim is 'whole' and unreviewed. I called it doubtful, not not_credible: it is a week old, the convergence route (dyadic spacing from Theorem 1.1) is laid out explicitly, and no specific error has been found, but the jump to mu(pi)=2 is extraordinary. Its role is generated, because the README says an internal model produced the manuscripts and no human author is named. For Bai I chose 'assisted' over 'none' because 'proof development' is mathematics, even though the quote does not split it between the two models. That event is scope 'none' anyway.
judgement.doubts: openai-2026-10 and openai-math-017 are the same event (same manuscript and release date), split across two research stages, and I gave both identical answers. The README quote is about the whole repository ('vast majority'), not family 017 specifically. Humphreys' 'human-AI collaboration' does not say what Claude produced, so I answered none. Its scope is instances, so it is discarded either way.
